messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel Rourke was 37 when he finally came for treatment, a divorced financial analyst who had built a careful, high-functioning life on the surface and then, after months of sleeping badly and keeping himself braced for trouble, found he could no longer pretend that concentration alone would hold him together. The event that haunted him had happened years earlier, when he was taken captive during a work trip abroad and held in a cramped room for days that blurred into one another under fear, deprivation, and constant uncertainty. He did not describe the worst details easily, but he said enough to make clear why certain moments still hit him with the force of danger: the sudden silence after commotion in a room, the sound of children crying in an apartment courtyard, and physical affection that came too quickly or too close, like a hug from a colleague or a family member. Those moments did not merely remind him of the past; they put his body back on alert. When his niece cried at a Sunday dinner, Daniel felt his shoulders tighten and his attention snap outward, scanning doors, windows, and anyone nearby as if he needed to detect the next threat before it arrived. At home he found himself watching the hall after dark, checking locks twice, and lying awake because, as he put it, if he let himself fall asleep he might miss something. The feelings of being on guard inside his own apartment were strongest in the evenings, when the city outside would go quiet and the absence of ordinary noise made him tense instead of relieved.

Over time, those moments of alarm became linked to the way he understood himself. Daniel had come to believe that something in him had been broken by what he endured, and that he had acted in ways that went against who he was simply to survive. He spoke with shame about having cooperated when he felt he should have resisted, and about the humiliating certainty that he had been reduced to an object, handled and directed rather than treated as a person. He was equally bitter that the people responsible had faced no consequences, which made the whole ordeal feel unfinished and insultingly unjust. When the memories surfaced, they did so with unusual force: he could see the room with startling clarity, down to the worn pattern on the floor and the angle of light across the wall, and he said the memories felt more real and vivid than ordinary things, as if they were still happening while everyday life had started to look flat and distant by comparison. Once, after catching a faint smell from a hallway steam pipe that reminded him of damp concrete and stale air from confinement, he felt the memory come back not just in pictures but in scent, vivid and bodily, and afterward he found himself more convinced that he had been permanently marked by the experience.

Those appraisals fed back into his daily reactions. Because he felt tainted, objectified, and furious that no one had been held accountable, Daniel became even more sensitive to anything that made him feel trapped, exposed, or touched without warning. A child crying in the waiting area of his building, a friend reaching for a congratulatory hug, or even a stretch of silence after the television went off could all make him feel that the old danger was close again. He would tense, pull away, and watch the room more carefully, and the more he monitored for threat, the more raw and convincing the memories became. Then, with the memories came the same sense that he had failed himself and that the world had failed to punish the men who hurt him, which in turn made him more likely to read ordinary contact or quiet as ominous. In this way, the reactions in his home and at work settled into a tightening pattern: he sat near the exit in conference rooms, avoided family gatherings where children were present, and kept his apartment unnaturally still in the evening, half-listening for signs of danger. As a divorced man living alone, he had plenty of opportunity to notice how much effort it took to feel safe in spaces that should have been his own, and that realization only deepened the sense that he was no longer living as himself.

He came for help after his sleep worsened and he found himself snapping to attention at the smallest sound, exhausted by the need to stay alert and frightened by how small his world had become. What he most wanted was to stop feeling like prey in his own home and to believe that the memories, the shame, and the anger could loosen their grip without making him vulnerable again.
